claims.text: Crystal structure and phase homogeneity in noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles are governed by sequential reduction or decomposition of mixed precursors.
Different constituents of a mixed precursor can undergo decomposition at different temperatures.
Slower heating with intermediate temperature dwells synchronizes reduction or decomposition of the individual elements.
Kinetic delays between precursor reactions promote phase separation.
Kinetic delays between precursor reactions promote elemental segregation.
Kinetic delays between precursor reactions promote uncontrolled nanoparticle morphology.
Rapid precursor-reaction kinetics contribute to high thermal decomposition temperatures.
Sequential precursor decomposition or reduction produces transient intermediate phases.
Synchronizing precursor reactions prevents local compositional imbalances.
Local compositional imbalances cause phase segregation and morphological irregularities.
A synchronized reduction or decomposition pathway increases atomic interdiffusion and mixing.
Greater atomic interdiffusion and mixing promote a metastable single-phase solid solution instead of separate phases or elemental clusters.
Mediating individual decomposition kinetics reduces the driving force for secondary-phase formation.
Relative to rapid heating and cooling, a slowed ramp with intermediate dwells produces a more uniform single-phase crystal structure.
Relative to rapid heating and cooling, a slowed ramp with intermediate dwells reduces elemental segregation.
Relative to rapid heating and cooling, a slowed ramp with intermediate dwells improves control of nanoparticle morphology.
Relative to rapid heating and cooling, a slowed ramp with intermediate dwells lowers the effective onset temperature for thermal decomposition.
The proposed mechanism is most applicable when differences among precursor reduction or decomposition temperatures are moderate enough to be synchronized thermally.
Extreme differences in the reaction kinetics of individual elements limit the effectiveness of the thermal intervention.
Significant differences in mixing enthalpy limit the effectiveness of the thermal intervention.
